claims.text: A dual-modality computational approach can calculate lattice and electronic thermal transport separately.
The dual-modality approach will predict total thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than earlier conflated methods.
The target specimen is defect-free and has controlled, minimal oxygen content.
DFT-computed phonon dispersions combined with Green–Kubo or machine-learned-force-field methods can determine lattice thermal conductivity.
Electronic transport coefficients can be calculated from DFT-derived electronic states and separately estimated electron relaxation times.
The proposed model is to be evaluated from 300 to 1200 K, with additional tests below 200 K.
Highly pure samples with negligible defects and impurities will also have negligible defect and impurity scattering.
HfNbTaTiZr has a uniform, disordered solid-solution atomic structure.
The disordered solid-solution structure underpins the thermal transport properties of HfNbTaTiZr.
Separately evaluating phonon and electronic transport avoids errors caused by conflating the two contributions.
Separate carrier calculations capture distinct temperature dependences and scattering mechanisms, thereby improving total-conductivity predictions.
The approach will reduce total-thermal-conductivity prediction error by roughly 20–30% relative to previous analytical estimates.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are expected to be comparable below 200 K.
Thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr is expected to become lattice-dominated from 300 to 1200 K.
Earlier models conflated lattice and electronic heat transport and consequently had higher uncertainty and lower accuracy.
Earlier measurements or estimates gave total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K with significant error margins.
Improved predictive performance is limited to defect-free, oxygen-minimized HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
Impurities and microstructural defects will degrade the predictive performance of the approach.
Classical molecular dynamics and DFT approximations may inadequately capture extreme-low-temperature quantum effects.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20%, or failure to reproduce the proposed low-to-high-temperature carrier crossover, would falsify the hypothesis.
